title: Movable Type Is Born in Asia
summary: A Chinese craftsman named Bi Sheng had a brilliant idea: make every character its own little piece of baked clay, so the pieces could be rearranged and used again and again. Later, people in Korea cast letters out of metal, and in 1377 they printed a book called Jikji that still survives today. A Korean king even invented a whole new, easy alphabet so more people could read.

sections.heading: A Commoner with a Big Idea
paragraphs: Picture a busy Chinese city in the 1040s, during the Song dynasty. The streets are full of shops selling silk, tea, porcelain and printed books. In the back of one workshop, a man is pressing soft, sticky clay into small squares and carving a single character into each one with a fine blade. His name is Bi Sheng, and he is about to invent movable type.

Movable type means separate pieces, one for each character, that can be arranged to make a page, printed, and then taken apart and rearranged to make a completely different page. Compare that with a woodblock, where the whole page is carved as one piece and can only ever print that one page. With movable type, the same character can be used over and over in thousands of different books.

We know very little about Bi Sheng himself. He was a commoner, an ordinary person with no official rank, not a famous scholar or nobleman. We do not know exactly where he lived, though some historians link him to the area around Hangzhou or Hubei, and a tombstone found in Hubei province in 1990 has been suggested as his, though not everyone agrees. His life dates are often given as about 970 to 1051, but these too are uncertain.

So how do we know about him at all? Thanks to one curious, brilliant writer: Shen Kuo. Shen Kuo was a government official, astronomer, engineer, mapmaker and all-round scientist. Late in his life, around 1088, he retired to a garden estate he called Dream Brook, and wrote down hundreds of short notes on everything that fascinated him: fossils, magnetism, music, medicine, rainbows, inventions. The collection is called the Dream Pool Essays, and it is one of the great science books of medieval China. It is also where we find one of the first known written descriptions of the magnetic compass needle.

In one entry, Shen Kuo explains that during the Qingli reign period, which ran from 1041 to 1048, a commoner named Bi Sheng invented movable type. Shen Kuo describes the method so carefully that we can almost watch Bi Sheng at work. Without that single entry, Bi Sheng's name might have been lost forever. Shen Kuo also tells us that after Bi Sheng died, his type was kept by people Shen Kuo knew, who treasured it.

sections.heading: How Bi Sheng's Clay Type Worked
paragraphs: Here is the method, step by step, as Shen Kuo described it.

First, Bi Sheng made the type. He took sticky clay and carved one character on each small piece, with the character raised and backwards, just like on a woodblock. Each piece was thin, about as thin as the edge of a coin. Then he baked the pieces in a fire to make them hard. Baked clay is called ceramic, the same family of material as a flowerpot or a bathroom tile. So Bi Sheng's type is sometimes called ceramic type.

Second, he prepared the printing plate. He took a flat iron plate and covered it with a sticky mixture of pine resin, wax and paper ash. Then he set an iron frame on top of the plate, like the edge of a tray.
Third, he set the type. Inside the frame, he packed the characters tightly together in the right order, line after line, until the frame was full. A full frame made one page.

Fourth came the clever bit. He held the plate near a fire. The heat softened the wax and resin underneath, making them gooey. Then he pressed a smooth, flat board down on top of the type, which pushed all the pieces to exactly the same height, so the top surface was as flat as a whetstone. When the plate cooled, the wax and resin hardened again and held every character firmly in place, like tiles in cement. Now it could be inked and printed just like a woodblock.
And when the printing was finished? He warmed the plate again, the wax softened, and the type could simply be brushed or picked off with a hand, clean and ready to use again. Nothing was wasted.

Bi Sheng also thought like an efficient factory manager. He kept two formes, two trays of type, going at once. While one was being printed, the other was being filled with type for the next page. When the first was done, the second was ready, so the work never had to stop. Common characters, such as the little grammar words zhi and ye, appear many times on a page, so he made twenty or more copies of each. For rare characters that he did not have, he carved a new one on the spot and baked it in a straw fire.

To find characters quickly, he stored the type in wooden cases, sorted by how the characters sounded, using rhyme groups, with paper labels on each group. That is a little like sorting your toy bricks by color so you can find the right one fast.

Shen Kuo explained why Bi Sheng did not use wood. Wood has a grain, so it soaks up ink unevenly, and wood swells when it gets wet, so the pieces would come out uneven and stick to the wax. Baked clay did not have these problems. Shen Kuo also noted that printing just two or three copies with movable type was not quick. But for dozens, hundreds or thousands of copies, it was amazingly fast.

sections.heading: Wang Zhen's Spinning Tables
paragraphs: About 250 years after Bi Sheng, China was ruled by the Yuan dynasty, founded by the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan. In the town of Jingde, in what is now Anhui province, the local magistrate was a man named Wang Zhen. A magistrate was a bit like a mayor, judge and tax collector rolled into one. Wang Zhen was especially interested in farming and machines, and he was writing a giant book about agriculture.

Wang Zhen decided to try movable type, but made of wood. Remember that Bi Sheng had rejected wood because of its grain and swelling. Wang Zhen found ways around these problems. He had skilled craftsmen carve characters onto a smooth wooden board, then saw the board into separate pieces, one character each, and trim them all with a small saw and knife until they were the same height and size. To fix the type in a page, he packed the lines with thin strips of bamboo and wedged everything tight with small wooden pieces, instead of using wax.

The biggest problem was finding characters. Wang Zhen's set had tens of thousands of pieces. How could a typesetter find the right one among so many? His answer was wonderfully practical: two large round tables that could spin, a bit like a giant lazy Susan. The characters were arranged on them by rhyme group, following the official rhyme book used for examinations, and each one was numbered. One table held the main characters, and the other held the most common ones. A typesetter sat between them and turned the tables to bring the right section within reach. In Wang Zhen's own description, one person read out the numbers from a list while another picked the type. As he put it, the type comes to the person, rather than the person walking to the type.

In 1298, Wang Zhen used his wooden type to print a local history of Jingde county, a text of more than 60,000 characters. Around 100 copies were finished in about a month. That was fast work for the time. Proud of his system, he wrote a careful description of it and added it to his great farming book, the Nong Shu, which means Treatise on Agriculture, published in 1313. Because he wrote it down so clearly, his method could be copied by others.

Wooden movable type spread beyond China, too. In the Dunhuang caves that you visited in the last chapter, explorers found hundreds of wooden type pieces for the Uyghur language, a Turkic language of Central Asia, which are thought to date from around 1300. Uyghur uses an alphabet, so each piece of type could be a letter or a whole word. It is a hint that movable type was travelling along the Silk Road too.

In the late 1400s, Chinese printers in the Wuxi area, such as Hua Sui and his family, began printing books with bronze type. So by the end of the period in this chapter, China had experimented with type made of clay, wood and metal.

sections.heading: Korea Casts Metal Letters
paragraphs: Now we cross the Yellow Sea to Korea. In the 1200s Korea was ruled by the Goryeo dynasty, and it had some of the best metal workers in Asia. Goryeo craftsmen cast beautiful bronze bells, mirrors, Buddhist statues and coins. They also had a problem: they needed books, but many had been lost in wars, and Korea's Buddhist temples and royal court wanted copies of many different texts, each in small numbers.

Cutting a whole set of woodblocks for a book you only need twenty copies of is a big waste of effort. Movable type made more sense, and metal type would be stronger and longer-lasting than clay or wood. So Korean craftsmen began casting type from metal.

The earliest clue comes from a writer named Yi Gyu-bo. In a collection of his works, he mentions that a book of ritual rules called Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun, meaning Detailed Rites of Past and Present, was printed with metal type, in 28 copies, according to the record. That happened around 1234, while the Goryeo court was sheltering on Ganghwa Island from the Mongol invasions, the same invasions that destroyed the first Tripitaka Koreana. Sadly, no copy of that book survives, so we only know about it from the written record.

How did Korean craftsmen cast their type? Different methods were used over time. One method, described in the 1400s by the Korean scholar Seong Hyeon, went like this. First, characters were carved onto pieces of soft wood such as beech. These wooden characters were pressed into trays of fine, damp sand, leaving a character-shaped hollow. Then molten bronze was poured into channels in the sand, filling every hollow. When the metal cooled, the sand was broken away, and out came a branch of metal characters, like fruits on a stem. Each character was snapped off and filed smooth. Another method used carved beeswax shapes covered in clay, which were heated so the wax melted out, leaving a perfect mould. Experts think something like this wax method may have been used for Jikji.

Korean metal type was not quite like the type later made in Europe. The pieces were not all exactly the same height, and they were held in place with beeswax and later with bamboo and paper, so pages could sometimes come out a little uneven. And Korean printers usually rubbed the paper with a brush, just like with woodblocks, rather than using a press. Printing with metal also needed a different ink. Water-based ink tends to bead up on smooth metal, like rain on a car window, so Korean printers worked to develop inks that would stick better to their bronze type.

sections.heading: Jikji: The Oldest Surviving Metal-Type Book
paragraphs: Our next scene is Heungdeok Temple, just outside the city of Cheongju in central Korea, in the summer of 1377. Monks are busy in a workshop, arranging small bronze characters into pages and carefully rubbing paper across them. They are printing a book of Zen Buddhist teachings collected by a respected monk named Baegun, who had died a few years earlier. His students, the monks Seokchan and Daljam, are in charge, and the project is being paid for by a Buddhist nun named Myodeok.

The book's full title is very long, so everyone calls it by its short name: Jikji. On the last page, a printed note records that it was printed with cast metal type at Heungdeok Temple in the 7th month of 1377. That is about 78 years before the Gutenberg Bible was finished in Mainz.

If you look closely at the pages, you can see that this was not a perfect operation. Some lines lean a little. Some characters are printed more darkly than others, and a few are upside down or did not print fully. Those little wobbles are actually useful evidence: they show the pages really were made from separate pieces of type, not from a single carved block.

Jikji was printed in two volumes, but only the second survives, and it is missing its first page. Its journey since then has been a long one. In the late 1800s, a French diplomat in Seoul named Victor Collin de Plancy collected hundreds of old Korean books and took them to France, including Jikji. It was shown at the great Paris World's Fair of 1900. Later it was sold to a collector named Henri Vever, who left it to the National Library of France in his will. It entered the library's collections in 1952, where it is still kept today.

For years, few people realized how important it was. Then a Korean historian named Park Byeong-seon, who worked at the National Library of France, studied it closely and showed that it was the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type. It was displayed at an exhibition for the International Book Year in Paris in 1972, and the world took notice. In 2001, UNESCO added Jikji to its Memory of the World register. UNESCO even created a prize for protecting the world's documentary heritage called the UNESCO/Jikji Memory of the World Prize.

Many Koreans would love Jikji to come home, and there are ongoing discussions between Korea and France about it. Meanwhile, the city of Cheongju has built the Cheongju Early Printing Museum near the site where archaeologists in 1985 found remains of Heungdeok Temple, including a metal object inscribed with the temple's name, which confirmed where the temple had stood.

sections.heading: King Sejong and an Alphabet for Everyone
paragraphs: In 1392 a new dynasty, the Joseon, took over Korea, with its capital at Hanyang, today's Seoul. The Joseon kings believed books were essential for good government, and they took printing very seriously. In 1403, King Taejong set up an official type foundry, a workshop for casting type, and it produced a new set of bronze type known as Gyemija, named after the year in the traditional calendar. Over the following centuries the royal foundry cast many new sets of type.

Taejong's son became one of the most admired rulers in Korean history: King Sejong the Great, who reigned from 1418 to 1450. Sejong loved learning. He gathered top scholars into a research institute called the Hall of Worthies, and he supported inventions such as rain gauges, sundials and water clocks. In 1434 his foundry cast a famous, elegant set of type called Gabinja. Records say that improvements made under Sejong, such as making type that fitted together more tightly, allowed printers to produce many more pages in a day than before.

But Sejong noticed a deep problem. Koreans spoke Korean, but they wrote using Chinese characters, called Hanja in Korean. Korean and Chinese are very different languages, so writing Korean in Chinese characters was awkward. Learning thousands of characters took years of study, which only wealthy families with free time could afford. Most farmers, craftspeople and servants could not read or write at all. Printing more books did not help people who could not read them.

So Sejong did something extraordinary. He created a brand-new alphabet, designed from scratch specially for the Korean language. He presented it to his court around the end of 1443, and in 1446 he announced it to the country in a document called Hunminjeongeum, which means The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People. Today the alphabet is called Hangul.

In his preface, Sejong explained, in words that are often translated roughly like this, that because Korean differs from Chinese, many ordinary people had things they wanted to say but could not write them down, and that he felt sorry for them and so made twenty-eight new letters for everyone to learn easily and use every day.

Hangul is brilliantly scientific. Some of the consonant letters were designed to show the shape of the mouth, tongue or throat when making the sound. For example, the letter for the 'g' or 'k' sound shows the back of the tongue lifting to touch the back of the mouth, and the letter for 'm' is a square, like closed lips. Extra strokes are added to show related sounds. The vowels are built from three simple symbols: a dot for heaven, a flat line for earth and an upright line for a person. Letters are grouped into square blocks, one block per syllable, so written Korean looks neat and even, and fits nicely into printing.

Sejong's scholar Jeong In-ji wrote in the 1446 commentary that a clever person could learn the letters in a morning, and even a slower learner could manage it in about ten days. The original alphabet had 28 letters. Four have dropped out of use, so modern Korean uses 24 basic letters: 14 consonants and 10 vowels.

Not everyone was pleased. Some scholars argued that Korea should stick with Chinese characters, the language of learning across East Asia, and many educated people kept writing in Chinese for centuries. In 1504 a cruel king, Yeonsangun, even banned the use of Hangul for a time after people used it to write criticisms of him. But Hangul survived, especially among women, merchants and ordinary readers, and today it is a great source of national pride. In South Korea, 9 October is celebrated as Hangul Day.

sections.heading: Why Movable Type Did Not Sweep China
paragraphs: Here is a puzzle. China invented movable type around 1040, about 400 years before Europe. Korea cast metal type by the 1200s. So why didn't movable type quickly take over all printing in East Asia, the way it later took over in Europe?

The first reason is the number of characters. A European printer needs only a few dozen letters, plus capitals, numbers and punctuation. But Chinese uses thousands of different characters, and a good printer needed many copies of the common ones. Wang Zhen's set ran to tens of thousands of pieces. Making, sorting, storing and finding so many pieces took a great deal of work and space. Even with spinning tables, it was a giant job.

The second reason is that woodblocks were good, cheap and flexible. Wood was easy to find, and carvers were skilled and not expensive to hire. A woodblock could hold text and pictures together, and it could be stored and reprinted whenever new copies were needed. With movable type, once a page was printed, the type was taken apart; if you wanted more copies a year later, you had to set the whole page all over again. For many publishers, printing small batches over many years made woodblocks the smarter choice.

The third reason is that East Asian printing was mostly done by hand-rubbing, not with a heavy press. That worked very well with wood and water-based ink, but less well with metal type, where a press and oily ink would have helped. In Korea, metal type was mainly used by the royal foundry to print official books and classics in fairly small numbers, rather than by many competing businesses selling cheap books to the public.

Movable type did not disappear, though. Chinese printers kept using wooden and bronze type for some projects. In the 1700s, the Qing dynasty emperor Qianlong ordered a huge set of more than 250,000 wooden type pieces to print a large collection of rare books, and earlier in that century a gigantic encyclopedia had been printed with bronze type. Both methods, woodblocks and movable type, existed side by side for centuries.

It is a great lesson about inventions. The best technology is not always the newest one. It is the one that fits the job, the language, the materials and the money available. In East Asia, woodblocks fitted beautifully. In a place with a small alphabet, plenty of customers and a tradition of screw presses, movable type would fit even better.
And meanwhile, far to the west in Europe, books were still being copied by hand, one letter at a time. Universities were growing, merchants were learning to read, and demand for books was exploding.

deepDive: Who invented movable type? On the evidence, the honor belongs to Bi Sheng in China in the 1040s, and the first metal movable type to Goryeo Korea, with a recorded use around 1234 and the surviving Jikji of 1377. Gutenberg's achievement in the 1450s was different: a complete system for casting large numbers of precisely uniform type with a hand mould, an oil-based ink and a screw press, built for an alphabet of a few dozen letters and a commercial market. Historians still debate whether knowledge of Asian printing reached Europe. Paper and block-printed playing cards and paper money certainly travelled west, and the Mongol Empire linked Eurasia in the 1200s and 1300s, but no document shows Gutenberg knew of Korean or Chinese type, and most scholars treat his work as an independent invention. Other debates concern the evidence itself. Bi Sheng is known almost entirely from one passage by Shen Kuo, so details of his life are uncertain. Some researchers have doubted whether fired clay type could have worked well; modern experiments and Tangut Buddhist texts from Western Xia that show features of clay type suggest it could. In Korea, a 2022 study argued that one surviving Buddhist text, Song of Enlightenment, may have been printed with metal type around 1239, which would make it older than Jikji; this claim is not universally accepted. Finally, the economics: movable type has a high fixed cost (thousands of sorts) but a low cost per new title, while woodblocks have a high cost per title but keep the page ready for reprinting. With thousands of Chinese characters and a market that bought books in small, repeated batches, woodblocks were often the rational choice. Hangul shows another route to cheap reading: reducing the number of symbols, rather than speeding up the copying of them.
funFact: Jikji, the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, was printed in Korea in 1377 and is kept today in the National Library of France in Paris.
